props.title: Limite
props.initialSlug: Lost souls adrift in time and memory

sections.content: Limite stands as Brazilian cinema's most ambitious experimental masterpiece. Director Mário Peixoto, only 22 when he made it, created a hypnotic meditation on human isolation that rivals the visual poetry of Un Chien Andalou (1929) and The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928). The film's mesmerizing rhythm follows three characters adrift at sea, using revolutionary camera movements and montage techniques that influenced Latin American cinema for decades. Sergei Eisenstein praised its innovative editing, while Georges Sadoul declared it one of the most important films ever made.

sections.content: The film's restoration history reads like a thriller. For decades, Limite existed only in deteriorating prints, nearly lost to time until Walter Salles and Martin Scorsese helped fund its preservation in the 1990s. Its influence echoes in later experimental landmarks like Meshes of the Afternoon (1943) and the Brazilian Cinema Novo movement, particularly Black God, White Devil (1964). The way Peixoto uses close-ups of hands, water, and machinery created a visual language that would inspire directors like Glauber Rocha and Nelson Pereira dos Santos.

The technical achievements of Limite were decades ahead of their time. Cinematographer Edgar Brazil pioneered tracking shots and extreme angles that wouldn't become common until the French New Wave. The film's abstract approach to narrative, focusing on mood and rhythm over traditional plotting, parallels the work of Jean Epstein in The Fall of the House of Usher (1928) and anticipates later experimental narratives like Last Year at Marienbad (1961). sections.content: Contemporary Brazilian filmmakers continue drawing inspiration from Limite. The dreamlike sequences in City of God (2002) and the experimental segments of Central Station (1998) show clear traces of Peixoto's influence. Even international directors like Carlos Reygadas, particularly in Silent Light (2007), echo Limite's contemplative pacing and focus on natural elements as metaphor.
